hook.text: Nearly every analyst loop has a spreadsheet round, because that's where quick analysis still happens. The questions are rarely about menus. They're about what a formula does when you copy it, sort it, or point it at the wrong column.

plan.text: Eighteen questions. We'll work the first ten on one small sheet of orders and a product list, then take the last eight a formula at a time.

pivot-in.text: First, the tool that answers a lot of them with no formula at all.

pivot.text: Question one. What is a pivot table, and when do you use one?

pivot-what.text: It summarizes a flat table: it groups the rows into categories and aggregates the values. It's GROUP BY that you can drag. Rows and columns hold the groups, values hold the sum, count or average, and filters narrow it down. Use it to explore, or to cross-tab in seconds.

crosstab.text: Question two. How would you build revenue by region and month? Region in rows, month in columns, revenue in values, summed. North in March is two ninety.

crosstab-count.text: It's the same matrix that sum of case when builds in SQL. Switch the summary to count, and that cell says two: two orders made up the two ninety.

lookup-in.text: Most of what comes next is about finding one value in another table.

lookup.text: Question three. What is V lookup, and what are its limits?

lookup-what.text: V lookup, short for vertical lookup, finds a key in the first column of a range and returns a value from a column to its right, by number. P one oh two, column three: nine dollars.

lookup-limits.text: It only looks right. Ask it for the mug's stock-keeping unit, its SKU, and it searches the SKU column for the word mug, and comes back NA: not available. And that column number is typed in. Insert a category column, and column three is now the category: the mug's price comes back as kitchen.

index.text: Question four. How does index match work, and why is it more robust?

xlookup.text: Question five. What does X lookup improve over both?

approx-in.text: Which brings up the argument everyone forgets.

approx.text: Question six. What's the difference between exact and approximate match?

approx-what.text: Exact returns only a precise hit. Approximate assumes the first column is sorted, and returns the largest value that isn't above the key. That's right for tiers: an order of six hundred forty lands in the five hundred tier, ten percent off.

approx-trap.text: And it's silently wrong for codes like these.

refs-in.text: Then, what happens when you copy a formula.

refs.text: Question seven. Explain absolute, relative and mixed references.

refs-fill.text: A relative reference shifts when you copy it. An absolute one, with dollar signs, stays put. Fill down A two times dollar F dollar one, and every row uses the tax rate in F one. Leave the dollars off, and the next row multiplies by F two, an empty cell: zero tax.

refs-mixed.text: A mixed reference locks one side. The cross-tab formula locks the region's column and the month's row, so one formula fills the whole grid.

iferror.text: Question eight. What does if error do, and when should you avoid it?

iferror-what.text: It swaps an error for a fallback, so a report stays clean. P one oh nine isn't in the table, so unknown is honest.

iferror-trap.text: But it hides every error the same way. A key with a stray space, and a formula that asks for a fourth column the table doesn't have, both come back unknown. Fix the cause first, and catch only what you expect.

tool-in.text: Two questions about when not to use a spreadsheet at all.

tool.text: Question nine. When should you use a spreadsheet, and when SQL or a database?

tool-when.text: A spreadsheet wins for quick exploration, small data, and something to hand a stakeholder. Move to SQL when the data outgrows it, well before a million rows, when the work has to be repeatable and audited, or when it joins several tables. If you redo the same manual steps every week, it belongs in SQL.

risks.text: Question ten. What are the main risks of analysis in a spreadsheet? Manual steps nobody can rerun. Formulas that break quietly when rows move. No schema: one revenue typed as text drops out of the sum, and the total reads ten seventy instead of twelve twenty. And big files that crawl, then crash.

rapid-in.text: The last eight each fit in a single cell.

r-sumif.text: Sum if adds the values that meet one condition, and sum ifs several. North sums to five sixty, and North in March to two ninety.

r-countif.text: Count if and count ifs count them instead: three North orders are over a hundred. Average if does means, and North averages one forty.

r-clean.text: Trim strips the extra spaces, and proper fixes the case: the messy name comes back as Ava Smith.

r-split.text: Left with find splits at a character: everything before the at sign is the username. Text join puts the pieces back, and skips the blanks.

r-dates.text: A date is stored as a serial number of days. March first, twenty twenty-four, is forty-five thousand three hundred fifty-two, so March thirty-first minus March first is thirty. A date stored as text won't sort or subtract until date value converts it.

r-format.text: Conditional formatting colors cells by a rule. Over a hundred fifty, and two orders light up. Use it to scan, not instead of a chart.

r-named.text: A named range gives a cell a name, so A two times tax rate reads as what it means, and still points at F one.

r-dupes.text: And to find duplicates, count each value against its own column: a count over one flags the repeated email.

next.text: A good table answers the question. A good chart gets someone to believe it. Next: data visualization.

index-match.text: Match finds the position of a value in one range.

index-left.text: Index returns what sits at that position in another. So it can look left: find mug among the names, and return its SKU.

index-ranges.text: And it points at ranges, not a column number, so after the insert the price range moves with the data, and P one oh two still costs nine.

xlookup-newer.text: It's the newer lookup, in Excel three sixty-five and twenty twenty-one or later; older versions don't have it.

xlookup-what.text: A lookup array and a return array, so any direction, in one function. Exact match by default. And a built-in if not found: P one oh nine says not found, with no if error around it.

approx-leave.text: Leave off false, and V lookup falls back to approximate. Look up P one oh five, which doesn't exist.

approx-lamp.text: Instead of NA, you get the lamp's price: twenty-four dollars. On unsorted data, it gets worse.

iferror-ifna.text: If NA catches only the not-available error: it takes the missing key, and lets the broken formula show.

r-clean-keys.text: Tidy the keys before you look up, or they won't match.

r-dupes-both.text: It flags both copies, so check them before Remove Duplicates, which keeps the first.

index-second.text: Mug is second, and the zero asks for an exact match.

iferror-space.text: But the stray space is a missing key too, so it stays hidden: trim it first.
